analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare drug plans from changing their covered-drug lists in the middle of a year.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2010, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Part D drug plans publish a 'formulary' — the list of prescription drugs they cover and on what terms. This one-page bill would have required any change to that list to take effect only at the start of a plan year, so seniors could not lose coverage for a drug or see its price shift in the middle of a year they had already picked a plan based on. The bill went to two House committees and a health subcommittee and was never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who chose a Part D plan based on the drugs it covered at enrollment. Under the bill, a plan could not drop their drug from the covered list, move it to a pricier tier, or impose new restrictions until the next annual enrollment period, when they would have a chance to switch plans.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Part D plan formularies to change only at the beginning of a plan year, so the terms people signed up for hold for the full year [S2][S3].
Protects people from mid-year surprises like a covered drug being dropped or moved to a higher-cost tier after they have already committed to a plan for the year [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Part D plan insurers (and, indirectly, drug manufacturers competing for formulary placement) lose the flexibility to adjust their drug lists mid-year, for example to steer patients to newly negotiated drugs or trim expensive ones without waiting for the annual cycle.

drawbacks.text: Plans and drug makers use mid-year formulary changes to respond to new evidence and new drugs; freezing lists for a full year can slow a plan's ability to drop a drug shown to be unsafe or ineffective, or to add a better new one [S2].
Locking in formularies for the plan year can push costs toward premiums for everyone in the plan, since plans lose a tool for managing drug spending during the year [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and narrow: seniors who buy a plan based on its drug list keep that deal for the year. The cost is that plans and insurers lose flexibility to adjust coverage mid-year, which could raise premiums slightly or delay the removal of bad drugs. For a single-page rule aimed at a well-documented complaint — losing access to a drug after choosing a plan that covered it — the trade-off favors beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and then a health subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress and was never taken up.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Schauer (D-MI) introduced the bill on March 23, 2010 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees the same day [S5].
Six days later it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Part D insurers keep their freedom to change covered-drug lists and cost terms in the middle of a year, and beneficiaries continue to bear the risk of losing a drug they enrolled under. The bill's sponsor lost his seat in the November 2010 election, and the measure died with the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Part D insurers keep mid-year flexibility

for.name: Rep. Mark Schauer (D-MI)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill barring mid-year Part D formulary changes; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 23, 2010, sent it to its Health Subcommittee on March 29, and never reported it out.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for the provisions in its jurisdiction and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of any opposition was never recorded; the bill died in committee with the sponsorship of a single member.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped plans' ability to change their covered-drug lists or cost terms mid-year, a tool plans use to manage drug spending. Beneficiaries who lose a drug mid-year bear the cost when that tool is used.

Mid-year formulary moves can drop a manufacturer's drug or shift it to a costlier tier; a freeze cuts both ways, but it also removes plans' ability to steer patients toward newer, cheaper drugs within the year. The direct effect on drug makers is smaller than on the plans.
